26 The diagram shows part of a stationary wave on a string.
X and Y are points on the string. The vibrations at X and Y are 180 out of phase.

hints: Look at the dashed envelopes: X is at the centre of one loop and Y is at the centre of the next loop, with a node on the string between them.
Recall the phase rule for a stationary wave: all points in the same loop are in phase, while points in adjacent loops move oppositely and are $180^{\circ}$ out of phase.
Recall that the length of one loop from node to node is half a wavelength, so compare the X to Y spacing with that node to node length.
walkthrough: Identify the diagram features: the solid line is the equilibrium string and the dashed lines are the extreme positions. X and Y are at antinodes where displacement is maximum.
State the stationary wave rule: points within one node-to-node loop vibrate in phase, and points in neighbouring loops vibrate in antiphase, meaning $180^{\circ}$ phase difference.
Check the given information: X and Y are $180^{\circ}$ out of phase, which matches them being in adjacent loops, as drawn with one node between them.
Relate loop length to wavelength: in a stationary wave the distance from one node to the next node is $\lambda/2$.
The distance from one antinode to the adjacent antinode is also one loop length, so $XY = \lambda/2$. This is option B.

A.explanation: A quarter wavelength is the node to antinode distance, not the distance between the two antinodes X and Y.

B.explanation: X and Y are antinodes of adjacent loops, so they are $180^{\circ}$ out of phase and separated by half a wavelength.

C.explanation: One wavelength would separate X from the next-but-one loop, which would vibrate in phase with X, not $180^{\circ}$ out of phase.

D.explanation: Two wavelengths is four times too large and would span four loops, not two adjacent antinodes.
